findings.text: Complaint text may reveal special-category data (for example, health or political information). For names, document the customer-support purpose and an Article 6 legal basis; limit access and retention to what that purpose needs.
For order numbers, confirm they are necessary for resolving tickets and set a retention period tied to that purpose; do not retain them longer than necessary.

India is a third country. Before any transfer, establish and document an available Chapter V route—typically appropriate safeguards if no applicable adequacy decision—and confirm enforceable rights and effective remedies; do not rely on the contract alone as proof of transfer compliance.

Update the relevant privacy information to identify the vendor/recipient category and disclose the India transfer and applicable transfer safeguards.
Record the India transfer, recipient, erasure periods where known, and security measures in the processing record; record the transfer in the transfer log as well.
Assess the vendor’s security measures, including access controls, encryption, resilience, and security testing, in light of ticket data and transfer risks.

next_steps: Confirm what complaint text may contain, and implement a way to prevent or redact special-category data unless an Article 9(2) condition is established; obtain DPO review before build if such data is involved.
Document the legal basis, purpose, ticket-data minimisation, retention schedule, and access model for names, order numbers, and complaint text.
Verify the specific transfer route and safeguards for the vendor and any subprocessors before tickets are transferred; add required transfer terms to the contract and record the transfer.

Update privacy information and the processing record/transfer log; determine whether ticket volume, sensitivity, or other features make the processing likely to result in high risk and require a DPIA.

assessment.title: Automated BNPL credit scoring and US fraud-vendor sharing
assessment.summary: The fully automated rejection of BNPL applicants is a significant-impact decision, and the description does not establish a valid GDPR Art. 22 exception and required safeguards. Credit scoring is high-risk AI; a DPIA and, before deployment, a fundamental-rights impact assessment are required. Register lookup found no matching entry.

findings.text: Do not launch fully automated rejections as described. Such decisions fall under Art. 22; redesign for meaningful human decision-making or establish a valid exception (contract necessity, law, or explicit consent) and, where applicable, safeguards including human intervention, the right to express a view and contest the decision.
Transaction history: document the lawful basis and demonstrate that the history used is necessary and proportionate for this scoring purpose; limit fields and retention accordingly.
Device fingerprint: treat device-linked identifiers as potentially personal data; document necessity and lawful basis, and minimise collection and retention.
Browsing behaviour: it can constitute profiling. Justify its necessity and lawful basis separately, and explain the profiling, data source, logic and consequences to applicants.
Complete a DPIA before processing: systematic automated evaluation used for decisions with significant effects requires one.
The creditworthiness scoring system is high-risk AI. Before first use, complete the deployer fundamental-rights impact assessment and notify the market surveillance authority of its results.
Assign competent, trained and authorised human oversight, and inform applicants that they are subject to the high-risk AI system when it makes or assists decisions about them.

Provide applicants with information on the processing, including the existence of automated decision-making, meaningful information about its logic, significance and consequences, and applicable data sources and rights.
The US fraud-prevention vendor’s transfer is covered by the organisation’s stated EU-US Data Privacy Framework certification fact; record each transfer in the transfer log.

next_steps: Redesign the rejection flow or establish and document an applicable Art. 22 exception and safeguards before build; obtain DPO review before build.
Assess and justify each input separately, especially whether device fingerprints and browsing behaviour are necessary; define minimisation and retention limits.
Complete the DPIA and the AI Act fundamental-rights impact assessment before launch; handle the required notification.
Prepare applicant notices and operational human-oversight arrangements; verify the vendor’s relevant certification status and log each transfer.

assessment.summary: This overdraft creditworthiness system is high-risk under the AI Act. Human approval can keep the final decision outside GDPR Article 22’s solely automated-decision rule only if the credit officer genuinely evaluates the recommendation and can change it; before launch, resolve reuse of repayment histories, complete impact assessments, and meet provider obligations arising from modification and own-brand deployment.

If the decision in practice becomes solely automated, Article 22 applies and its conditions and safeguards must be met.

assessment.title: Selfie-to-ID biometric identity verification for account opening
assessment.summary: Face matching for unique identification processes special-category biometric data and needs an Article 9 ground; the optional agent route may support freely given explicit consent, but the design does not establish that consent or its safeguards. Complete a DPIA before processing, and ensure a failed match cannot lead to a consequential decision without the required safeguards and an effective human route. The one-to-one verification described is excluded from the AI Act Annex III biometrics high-risk category when used solely to confirm the customer’s claimed identity.

findings.text: The selfie-to-ID match is biometric processing for unique identification. Do not run it unless customers give valid, informed, specific and freely given explicit consent; make the video-call option genuinely equivalent, with no disadvantage for choosing it, and provide a way to withdraw consent.

If a negative match automatically refuses account opening or otherwise significantly affects the customer, do not make that solely automated decision without a valid Article 22 exception and safeguards, including effective human intervention and a way to contest it. The offered video-call route must not be the only remedy if customers cannot reasonably access it.

Document and communicate an Article 6 legal basis for the selfie, ID scan and match-result processing; Article 9 explicit consent does not replace this requirement. Explain purposes, retention periods and the consequences of not providing the data before collection.
Complete a DPIA before launch, covering biometric matching, false matches and failures, the ID scan, and the alternative agent route; set out necessity, proportionality, risks and safeguards.

Set and justify a retention period for the retained ID document scan and yes/no result, and delete them when no longer necessary. Keeping the full scan needs a necessity justification and access controls.
Deleting face templates immediately after matching limits their storage as described; verify deletion from temporary storage, logs and any processor systems as well as the main system.

On the described purpose—one-to-one confirmation that the customer is the person shown on their ID—the biometric verification use is excluded from the AI Act Annex III point 1(a) remote biometric identification category; this conclusion depends on keeping that purpose and scope narrow.

next_steps: Design and document the explicit-consent flow, including the genuinely equivalent video-call alternative, information provided, and withdrawal handling; confirm applicable national rules do not prevent reliance on consent.
Identify and document the Article 6 legal basis for each processing purpose and set retention schedules for the ID scan and result.
Complete the DPIA and obtain DPO review before build, as required for this biometric-data feature.
Specify the consequences of a failed match and implement human intervention and contest mechanisms before any consequential refusal.
Test and document deletion of face templates across all systems, including processor systems, logs and backups; limit access to retained scans and results.
Keep use strictly one-to-one for identity confirmation and check whether any component qualifies as an AI system.

assessment.title: Self-service account deletion and erasure workflow
assessment.summary: Do not implement an unconditional, immediate wipe: erasure rights do not override personal-data retention required by law, and high-risk AI logs under the deployer’s control generally must be kept for at least six months. findings.text: Change the unconditional wipe of credit-scoring audit logs. Where logs are under your control, keep them for at least six months (unless applicable law provides otherwise); after that, retain only as long as appropriate and lawful.

Transaction history: do not delete records still required by a binding AML law during the stated five-year period. Confirm the policy reflects an applicable legal obligation; an internal policy alone does not establish the erasure exception, and erase or minimise records once the legal need ends.

Identity data: do not promise to erase every identity field where a minimal link is necessary to retain legally required transaction records or AI logs. Map which identifiers are necessary for those records, restrict them to that purpose, and erase the rest when no longer needed.

Replace immediate blanket deletion with a request workflow that checks which data are eligible for erasure and handles any exception. Erase eligible data without undue delay, and tell the requester what action was taken within one month; do not equate this with an unconditional instant wipe.
